processing: As a plain infusion, buds of Japanese honeysuckle are simply dried. A separate scented style layers the flowers with true tea in a process similar to jasmine tea.
harvest_season: Honeysuckles flower profusely in early summer; as a herb, unopened buds are the usual prized picking.
appearance_dry: Slim, curved buds in cream, pale gold and light green, like tiny dry trumpets.
appearance_wet: Buds swell and soften into pale, slender tubes.
taste_profile: Sweet, floral nectar on the nose over a light herbal body, as is typical of dried honeysuckle, with a little bitterness if overbrewed.

brewing.notes: Steep by the mug or in a glass pot. Slightly cooler water keeps the sweet aroma; long boiling is for medicine rather than for drinking pleasure.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage. Plain buds are a yearly summer crop, best in the first year while the aroma lasts. A scented tea made with honeysuckle is sold like other scented teas, and it contains caffeine because of the base leaf.
description:
Honeysuckle tea is a simple infusion of dried buds of Lonicera japonica, the plant known in Chinese as jin yin hua, gold and silver flower. The name comes from a bloom that opens white and turns yellow. In Japan the same plant goes by nindo. Fengqiu in Henan is one of the places it is associated with.

There are two different products under this name. One is the plain dried bud, which has no caffeine. The other is true tea scented with the flowers, a method close to jasmine scenting.

The plain infusion smells sweet and flowery, with little body and a faint bitter edge if left too long, as is typical of dried honeysuckle. Use a modest amount and hot rather than boiling water, and enjoy it in summer or chilled.

Look for clean, whole, unopened buds with a fresh scent, and avoid dull brown lots. It has a place in traditional Chinese medicine, and the plant is grown commercially for it, so anyone taking it as a remedy should ask a doctor. As a garden plant it is invasive in many countries, so foraging abroad needs careful identification, since other honeysuckle species have poisonous berries.
history:
Japanese honeysuckle is native to East Asia and is grown as a commercial crop for traditional Chinese medicine. Using honeysuckle to scent tea, by a process similar to jasmine tea, was popularised in the Qing dynasty.

When the plain bud infusion became an everyday drink is less clearly recorded, though it remains well known as a summer drink.
